theory.intro: A **conversion graph** is a straight line used to change one unit into another, and its gradient is the conversion rate. Some conversion lines pass through the origin; others, like Celsius to Fahrenheit, do not, because $0^{\circ}\text{C}$ is not $0^{\circ}\text{F}$.
facts: In $y = kx + c$, the number $c$ is the value of $y$ when $x = 0$.

mastery.question_text: A recipe says to preheat an oven to $180^{\circ}$C. An older recipe, in Fahrenheit, says $350^{\circ}$F. Using the fact that the Celsius-to-Fahrenheit conversion line has gradient $1.8$ and crosses the $^{\circ}$F axis at $32$, determine which temperature is hotter.
mastery.solution_text:
$F = 1.8C + 32$
$= 1.8(180) + 32$
$= 356$
Since $356^{\circ}\text{F} > 350^{\circ}\text{F}$, the $180^{\circ}$C oven setting is hotter.

mastery.question_text:
A conversion graph between Australian dollars ($x$) and Canadian dollars ($y$) is a straight line through the origin.
One point on the line is $(140, 154)$.
Find the exchange rate, then convert $\$60$ AUD to CAD.
mastery.solution_text:
$m = \dfrac{154}{140}$
$= 1.1$
The exchange rate is $1.1$ CAD per AUD.
$60 \times 1.1$
$= 66$
$\$60$ AUD $= \$66$ CAD

mastery.question_text:
A conversion graph for $^{\circ}$C to $^{\circ}$F passes through $(0, 32)$ and $(100, 212)$.
A student claims the gradient represents 'how many degrees Fahrenheit the temperature rises for every one-degree rise in Celsius.' Find the gradient and decide if the student is correct.
mastery.solution_text:
$m = \dfrac{212 - 32}{100 - 0}$
$= \dfrac{180}{100}$
$= 1.8$
The student is correct: the gradient is the rate of change, so a rise of $1^{\circ}$C always corresponds to a rise of $1.8^{\circ}$F, regardless of the $y$-intercept.
